questions.question: How do you raise exceptions in Ruby?
questions.title: Raising Exceptions in Ruby
questions.direct_answer: raise throws an exception: raise 'something broke' (raises a RuntimeError with that message), raise ArgumentError, 'expected a string' (raises a specific class), raise SomeError.new('msg', extra: x) (with a custom object). You raise when a precondition is violated (a nil arg where a value is required, an impossible state, a failed business rule) — not for normal control flow. The caller then rescues it. raise with no class raises RuntimeError; with a class, that class; with an instance, that instance. Pair raise with a specific class (or custom exception) so the caller can rescue the right thing.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the forms of raise (message -> RuntimeError, class+message, instance) and when to raise (violated precondition, not flow).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Raising for normal control flow (use a return value), or raise with no class (RuntimeError) where a specific class fits.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: raise 'msg' (RuntimeError), raise Class, 'msg', raise Instance. Raise on a violated precondition, not for normal flow; pick a specific class.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: raise 'msg' raises a RuntimeError; raise Class, 'msg' raises a specific class.
raise Instance raises a custom object (with extra fields).
Raise on a violated precondition (nil arg, impossible state, failed business rule).
Don't raise for normal control flow — use a return value (nil or a Result).
In a rescue, bare raise re-raises the same exception (preserves the backtrace).

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: raise throws an exception. raise something broke raises a RuntimeError with that message; raise ArgumentError, expected a string raises a specific class with a message; raise SomeError dot new with msg and extra raises a custom object with extra data. You raise when a precondition is violated — a nil argument where a value is required, an impossible state, a failed business rule — not for normal control flow, because exceptions are for exceptional cases and the caller then rescues it. raise with no class raises RuntimeError; with a class, that class; with an instance, that instance. Pair raise with a specific class or a custom exception so the caller can rescue the right thing instead of a generic RuntimeError. A common mistake is raising for normal control flow, when you should use a return value, and raise with no class where a specific class fits.

sections.title: Forms of raise
sections.content:
message -> RuntimeError; class + message; instance.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  M[raise 'msg'] --> R[RuntimeError]
  C[raise Class, 'msg'] --> S[that class]
  I[raise Instance] --> O[that instance]
```

sections.title: Raising exceptions
sections.content:
```ruby
# 1) raise with a message -> RuntimeError
raise 'expected a positive number'

# 2) raise a specific class + message
raise ArgumentError, 'expected a string' unless name.is_a?(String)
raise ArgumentError, 'count must be > 0' if count <= 0

# 3) raise a custom instance (with extra fields)
raise PaymentError.new('card declined', order_id: order.id)

# 4) re-raise the current exception (in a rescue)
begin
  work
rescue => e
  log(e)
  raise          # re-raise the SAME exception (preserves backtrace)
end

# Use raise for violated preconditions, NOT normal flow:
def divide(a, b)
  raise ArgumentError, 'divisor cannot be zero' if b == 0
  a / b
end
```
